body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students tell defining attributes (closed, number of sides and corners) from non-defining attributes (color, size, which way it is turned), and draw shapes with given attributes (1.G.A.1).
- Students compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, triangles, half-circles and quarter-circles) to make a new shape (1.G.A.2).
- Students partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares as halves, fourths and quarters, and understand that more equal shares make smaller shares (1.G.A.3).

MATERIALS
- Pattern blocks and paper shapes in several sizes and colors (triangles, squares, rectangles, half-circles, quarter-circles)
- Geoboards and rubber bands, or dot paper
- Paper circles and rectangles for folding, and scissors
- A "shape detective" sorting mat: Is it a triangle? Yes / No
- Tablets with the class activities open, for photos of work

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Shape Detectives together. Lesson activity: What Makes a Shape? Sort a pile of paper shapes into triangles and not triangles, including skinny, turned and open ones. Ask: what clue did you use?
Day 2: Build New Shapes. Students make new shapes with pattern blocks (two triangles make a square, a square and two triangles make a trapezoid), trace them, and record themselves telling which shapes they used.
Day 3: Fold paper circles and rectangles in half. Are the two parts the same size? Then fold again to make fourths. Name them: halves, fourths, quarters. Students start Halves and Fourths.
Day 4: Finish Halves and Fourths. Share a pretend pizza: is a half or a fourth bigger? Cut two same-size paper circles to check. Return to unequal shares: why is the bigger piece not a half?
Day 5: Assessment: Shapes and Shares Check. Read each problem aloud. Students may use pattern blocks and paper shapes.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give students shapes to hold and count sides and corners with a finger or sticker on each corner. Fold paper shapes before drawing lines.
- Support: for equal shares, start with rectangles, which are easier to fold evenly than circles.
- Stretch: find two different ways to cut a square into fourths (four small squares or four triangles); build one shape from as many smaller shapes as possible and count them.
- Multilingual learners: label each shape with its name and a picture. Teach side, corner, equal, half and fourth with hands-on folding. Note that "quarter" and "fourth" mean the same here.
- Watch for students who call a turned square a "diamond": it is still a square because its sides and corners did not change.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are shape detectives! We are learning that a shape's name comes from its sides and corners, not its color or size, and we are cutting shapes into halves and fourths. At snack time, ask your child to cut a sandwich or a tortilla into two equal shares, then four. Ask: which piece is bigger, a half or a fourth? Go on a shape hunt around the house too.
title: Teacher guide: Shapes and Equal Shares
